```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

The look of a Research Guide is not hard-coded — it is driven by a **design**: a
setting that maps each data type to the sequence of reporting functions used to
render it. Because the design is data, you can inspect it, and change it, without
touching the package.

## The design is a table of data type → reporting function

`get_design()` returns the active design as a data frame. Each row places one
piece of a variable's section:

```{r lib, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(datagoodr)
d <- get_design()
head(d)
```

The columns are the whole grammar:

- **TYPE** — the data type the row applies to (`number`, `categorical`,
  `boolean`, `temporal`, `text`, `identifier`).
- **DIV** — the slot in the section grid the piece is drawn into.
- **VNAME** — the DGF column the piece reads (`rg_stats`, `rg_graphics`,
  `dd_vdesc`, …).
- **LABEL** — the heading shown above it.
- **FUNCTION** — the **name of the reporting function** that renders that column.

Here is the full recipe for a **numeric** variable — the mapping that produced
the histogram and tables you saw in the other vignettes:

```{r number-design}
d[d$TYPE == "number", c("DIV", "VNAME", "LABEL", "FUNCTION")]
```

Read the last two rows: in slot `div8`, the `rg_graphics` column is rendered by
`paste_histogram`; in `div9`, `rg_stats` is rendered by `paste_stats_horizontal`.
Swap the type and the functions change — a `categorical` row sends `rg_graphics`
to `paste_treemap`, a `text` row to `v_to_wordcloud`.

## How the mapping is parsed and applied

Internally each layout is written as a compact string,
`"div ;; column ;; LABEL ;; function"`, and two helpers turn it into action:

- `parse_design()` splits those strings into the `DIV / VNAME / LABEL / FUNCTION`
  data frame above;
- at render time the **FUNCTION name is looked up and called** on the named DGF
  column (`parse_functions()` first checks every name resolves, so a typo fails
  loudly instead of rendering nothing).

So "aesthetics" reduces to a lookup: *for this type, draw this column, with this
function.* Change the lookup and you change the report.

## Customizing: change the functions, or change the mapping

**1. Override a reporting function.** Because the design stores a function *name*,
defining your own function of that name makes the guide call yours — no change to
the mapping. This is the usual way to restyle: redefine a renderer (or a
formatter such as `dollarize`) in your project's `DG.R`.

```{r override, eval=FALSE}
# in DG.R — restyle the numeric graphic without touching the design:
paste_histogram <- function(VNAME, LABEL = "HISTOGRAM") {
  # ... your own plot from the rg_graphics payload ...
}
```

**2. Change the mapping itself.** Pass a replacement layout to `get_design()`
(the same hook `create_rg()`'s scaffold uses). Here is a slimmed numeric section —
label, properties, and stats only, no histogram:

```{r custom-layout}
custom_number <- c(
  "div2 ;; dd_vlabel     ;;            ;; v_to_txt",
  "div7 ;; rg_properties ;; PROPERTIES ;; paste_properties",
  "div9 ;; rg_stats      ;; STATS      ;; paste_stats_horizontal"
)
d2 <- get_design(layouts = list(number = custom_number))
d2[d2$TYPE == "number", c("DIV", "VNAME", "LABEL", "FUNCTION")]
```

The numeric section is now three rows instead of nine, and the histogram is gone.
You can drop sections, reorder them, relabel them, or point a slot at a different
function — all by editing the character vector.

**3. Shadow a layout globally.** Defining `layout.numeric` (or
`layout.character`, `layout.logical`, …) in your session or `DG.R` shadows the
package default for that type, so every guide you render picks it up without
passing `layouts` each time.

## Where this fits

`create_rg()` scaffolds a project with a `DG.R` precisely so these overrides live
*beside* your data, not in the package — the design travels with the project and
the package stays untouched. For the functions a design points at, see *Data
Reporting Functions*.
